questions.stem: In an infraclavicular block, what extra step covers the medial upper arm skin supplied by the intercostobrachial nerve?
questions.answer: Extra subcutaneous injection on the medial arm just below the axilla

questions.stem: Which surgery is a main indication for an infraclavicular brachial plexus block?
options: Arm, elbow, forearm and hand surgery

questions.stem: Why was the infraclavicular block previously avoided?
questions.answer: Complex, variable landmarks, frequent vascular puncture and limited success

questions.stem: Why has ultrasound made the infraclavicular block more popular?
questions.answer: It shows the axillary artery and surrounding cords

questions.stem: Why is an infraclavicular block low risk for pneumothorax and neuraxial spread?
questions.answer: The needle is further from the pleura and neuraxis

questions.stem: With a lateral parasagittal approach to an infraclavicular block, how likely is phrenic nerve block?
What are the main downsides of an infraclavicular block?
questions.answer: Plexus is deeper and needle angle steeper, so needle and anatomy are harder to see together

questions.stem: In an infraclavicular block, do individual cords need to be targeted for success?
options: Yes, each cord must be injected separately
No, a U-shaped deposit around the artery is enough
Yes, only the posterior cord is needed
No, only the lateral cord is needed

questions.stem: What is the patient position for the paracoracoid (traditional) infraclavicular technique?
In the paracoracoid technique, why abduct the arm to 90 degrees with the elbow flexed?
questions.answer: It lifts the clavicle, makes the plexus shallower and improves views

questions.stem: In the paracoracoid technique, the linear probe sits parasagittally below the clavicle, just ____ to the coracoid process.
In the paracoracoid view, where does the axillary artery lie?
options: Deep to pectoralis major and minor and their fasciae

questions.stem: In the paracoracoid infraclavicular approach, how deep is the axillary artery typically?
Which brachial plexus block has its cords deepest, around 3–5 cm?
On a parasagittal infraclavicular view, where is the lateral cord relative to the axillary artery?
On a parasagittal infraclavicular view, where is the medial cord relative to the axillary artery?
On a parasagittal infraclavicular view, where is the posterior cord relative to the axillary artery?
On the parasagittal infraclavicular scan, why is the needle kept lateral to the pleura?
questions.answer: To reduce the risk of pneumothorax

questions.stem: What structure may be seen deep in the cephalad part of an infraclavicular parasagittal image?
Which vessels in the needle path may be checked with colour Doppler for an infraclavicular block?
options: Subclavian artery and internal jugular vein
Lateral thoracic artery and basilic vein

questions.stem: In the paracoracoid technique, where and in which direction is the needle inserted?
questions.answer: In-plane from the cephalad end of the probe, just below the clavicle, aimed caudad

questions.stem: In the paracoracoid technique, which side of the axillary artery does the needle reach first?
In the paracoracoid technique, what volume is given after aspiration to confirm placement?
In the paracoracoid technique, what is the endpoint of injection seen on ultrasound?
questions.answer: U-shaped spread around the artery: cephalad, caudad and posterior

questions.stem: In the paracoracoid technique, what should you do if septa limit spread around the artery?
questions.answer: Reposition the needle to complete the U

questions.stem: What is often mistaken for the posterior cord on infraclavicular ultrasound?
In infraclavicular ultrasound, what does the heel-up probe manoeuvre achieve?
questions.answer: It makes it easier to change the needle angle

questions.stem: In the retroclavicular (RAPTIR) approach, where and how does the needle enter?
questions.answer: Just cephalad and posterior to the clavicle, in-plane and parallel to the probe

questions.stem: In the retroclavicular (RAPTIR) approach, where should the needle be aimed?
options: Superficial to the artery, at 12 o'clock
Lateral to the artery, at 9 o'clock
Deep to the axillary artery, at 6 o'clock
Medial to the artery, at 3 o'clock

questions.stem: For a costoclavicular block, why abduct the ipsilateral arm to 90 degrees if possible?
options: It hides the clavicle from view

questions.stem: Where is the probe placed for a costoclavicular block?
options: Transverse over the axilla at mid-humerus
Transverse in the medial infraclavicular fossa, next to the clavicle

questions.stem: On costoclavicular ultrasound, where are the cords relative to the axillary artery?
In a costoclavicular block, where should the needle tip sit?
questions.answer: In the middle of the three cords, ideally between the lateral and posterior cords

questions.stem: In a costoclavicular block where a septum separates the lateral cord, what volume goes to the lateral cord?
What is the alternative needle path for a costoclavicular block?
options: Out-of-plane, from cephalad, into the axillary vein
Subcutaneous, from the lateral arm, into the deltoid
In-plane, medial to lateral, between the artery and lateral cord
Out-of-plane, from posterior, into the scapula

questions.stem: Below the clavicle, what does the brachial plexus form around the axillary artery?
In the landmark infraclavicular technique, where is the most common first mark made?
questions.answer: 2–3 cm caudad from the midpoint of the clavicle

questions.stem: In the landmark infraclavicular technique, at what angle is the needle directed towards the axilla?
In the landmark infraclavicular technique, what current should produce a hand motor response?
Why is the infraclavicular site well suited to continuous catheters?
questions.answer: Chest wall muscle holds the catheter and resists dislodgement better than shallower sites

questions.stem: In a continuous infraclavicular block, where should the catheter sit?
questions.answer: Near the cords, under the pectoral muscles

questions.stem: In a continuous infraclavicular block, which phases does ultrasound guide in most patients?
In a continuous infraclavicular block, which needle direction is used for the needle placement?
Before injecting and threading a continuous infraclavicular catheter, where should the tip be?
Which motor response from the posterior cord confirms needle position in a continuous infraclavicular block?
What is the typical starting infusion rate for a continuous infraclavicular catheter?
In a continuous infraclavicular block, what is the typical patient-controlled bolus size, given every hour?
